etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English clothen, from Old English *clāþian (“to clothe”), from Proto-Germanic *klaiþōną (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European *gley- (“to adhere to, stick”). Cognate with Dutch kleden, German kleiden, Swedish kläda, after apocope klä. See also cloth, clad.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To adorn or cover with clothing; to dress; to supply clothes or clothing.

quote.citation: c. 1590-92, William Shakespeare, The Taming of the Shrew‎[1], act IV, scene ii:
quote.text: Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 23:21:
quote.text: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.

quote.citation: 1766, [Oliver Goldsmith], The Vicar of Wakefield: […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), Salisbury, Wiltshire:  […]  B. Collins, for F[rancis] Newbery, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The naked every day he clad, / When he put on his clothes.

definitions.definition: (figurative) To cover or invest, as if with a garment.
